name: Question 19
problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14158590/assets/085e28508da725e445c410fedc08a1992dccc5e0a7b99b3248182f58ffae2c07.png)

Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=4z,$ shown above.
worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $2$ centered at $(0,0,2).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=4z$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =4z \\ {\rho }^{2} & =4\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho -4\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =4\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14158590/assets/8a730a72fe9f3f69878ef647215e8ed05e913f23bf8e0fab01bad6271e860335.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 4\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\rho }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{1}{\rho }\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{[\frac{1}{2}{\rho }^{2}]}_{\rho =0}^{\rho =4\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}\,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }d\theta  \\  & =8{[-\frac{1}{3}{cos}^{3}⁡ϕ]}_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi /2}\cdot [\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi } \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}(0-1)\cdot (2\pi -0) \\  & =\frac{16\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$
